meta.title: Who really said "Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — genuinely Confucius. It's Analects 2.15, and this exact English wording is James Legge's 1861 translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous'?
meta.ogDescription: A real Confucius line: Analects 2.15. This exact English phrasing is James Legge's 1861 translation, not Confucius's own words.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 551–479 BC · Chinese philosopher & teacher · English wording by translator James Legge (1815–1897)
answer.sourceLine: This is an authentic saying — the ‘Analects’ (‘Lúnýǔ’), Book 2, verse 15: “學而不思則罔，思而不學則殆.” The polished English — “Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous” — is James Legge’s 1861 translation ↗, not Confucius’s own words, which were in Classical Chinese.

source.excerpt: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
trail: The saying is Analects 2.15 ↗, with the Chinese “學而不思則罔，思而不學則殆” set beside Legge’s English.
The exact wording traces to James Legge’s translation of the Confucian Analects (1861) ↗, in his ‘Chinese Classics’ Vol. I.
Translation records show how much the English varies by hand — Ware (1950) has “Learning without thought ends in a blur,” per WIST’s catalogue of Analects 2.15 renderings ↗.
source.excerptNote: Legge’s 1861 English rendering of Analects 2.15. The bracing balance of the two clauses is partly Legge’s craft — other translators put it very differently.

source.rightsNote: The ancient Chinese text is long in the public domain, and James Legge’s English translation was first published in 1861 (‘The Chinese Classics’, Vol. I) — well before 1931 — so this specific wording is public domain in the United States. Note that a more recent translator’s wording of the same verse could still be in copyright.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: About Confucius
author.metaLine: 551–479 BC · Chinese philosopher, teacher & founder of the Confucian tradition
author.bio: Confucius (‘Kǒngzǐ’, Master Kong) was a philosopher and teacher of the Spring and Autumn period whose ideas on ethics, learning and social harmony shaped East Asian thought for millennia. He wrote no treatise himself; his teachings survive chiefly in the Analects, a collection of his sayings and dialogues compiled by disciples after his death. This aphorism pairs rote learning and untethered thought, arguing each is barren without the other.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a “Confucius said” line, this one is real. The catch is the English: the memorable phrasing belongs to a Victorian translator, and it circulates in a swarm of conflicting wordings.

items.who: Confucius — but not in these English words
items.scope: The polished sentence is James Legge’s
items.why: Confucius spoke Classical Chinese; the elegant “labour lost … perilous” balance is Legge’s 1861 English ↗. Quoting it as Confucius’s literal words skips the translator.

items.who: Countless paraphrases passed off as ‘the’ quote
items.why: The same verse appears as “Learning without thinking is useless; thinking without learning is dangerous” and other forms — WIST lists renderings from Jennings, Ku Hung-Ming, Waley, Lau and more ↗. No single English version is ‘the’ original.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is genuinely Confucius’s — Analects 2.15 ↗ — but this exact English sentence is James Legge’s 1861 translation.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Analects 2.15 is one of Confucius’s most quoted lines because it refuses a false choice: it faults empty book-learning (‘learning without thought’) and untethered speculation (‘thought without learning’) in the same breath, insisting the two must work together.

Its fame in English owes much to James Legge, the Scottish missionary-sinologist whose 19th-century translations made the Confucian classics accessible to Western readers — and whose crisp phrasing is what most people are actually quoting.
context.pull: Learning and thinking are faulted in the same breath — each barren without the other.
